wa_southeast_corner.blurb: The far southeastern part of Washington, where short basalt crags rise near the Columbia River and the Walla Walla country. Sport routes are the largest group, followed by bouldering and trad, with a little top-rope and ice. Routes are mostly 5.7 to 5.10, with a modest spread up through 5.12. Wallula Gap is the biggest venue: two basalt bands with brief, often one-move routes, a west-facing cliff that works year-round, and rock that can be loose in places. The Dikes is almost entirely sport, Granite Point mixes trad, sport and boulders, and Roadkill Crag leans trad. Expect quick, local-style climbing rather than long days on big walls.

bc_sea_to_sky_north_of_whistler.blurb: The Highway 99 corridor running north from Whistler through Pemberton and over toward Lillooet, in very mountainous terrain. Trad and sport routes lead, with bouldering close behind, and a smaller set of ice climbs, mostly WI2 to WI5, plus alpine and mountaineering objectives. Rock grades concentrate at 5.10 and 5.11, with fewer easier lines. The Pemberton Boulders are the largest cluster, Suicide Bluff is mainly trad, Lillooet Edge is mostly bolted, and Duffey Lake Road holds much of the ice. The high-mountain summer season is short, mostly August and September, while winter brings ice, mountaineering and backcountry skiing.

co_hartman_rocks.blurb: A granite recreation area just south of Gunnison, at roughly 8,000 feet, scattered with outcrops and boulders across open country. Bouldering is the biggest part, from very easy up to hard, followed by bolted sport routes from about 5.5 to 5.12 with plenty at 5.9 to 5.11, plus a handful of trad cracks and top-rope setups. The rock has been compared to Joshua Tree, solid in most places and loose or crumbly in others. Climbing is friendly and low-key and spread over a wide area. Sub-areas include Kill Hill, The Stash, The Beach and The Other Side, each with a different feel. Shared with trail users throughout.

az_senator_s_highway_areas_groom_creek.blurb: Bouldering only, in the foothills of the Bradshaw Mountains a short drive south of Prescott, at around 6,400 to 7,000 feet. Steel-grey, mid-grained boulders sit on a hillside among ponderosa pines. Groom Creek holds the large majority, with Wolf Creek, Hassayampa Creek and Goldwater Lake adding smaller groups. Variety is wide, from overhanging jug problems to slabby slopers. A huge share of the problems are very easy, with a good middle range and a tail of hard lines up to V10 and beyond. Landings are mostly good, but the layout at Groom Creek is complicated, so plan several visits to get your bearings.

ca_big_bear_south.blurb: Climbing on the south side of Big Bear Lake in the San Bernardino Mountains, around 7,600 to 7,800 feet. Bouldering is the biggest group, followed by trad, alpine-style routes and sport, with a few top-ropes. Roped climbs are mostly 5.9 to 5.12 with a heavy dose of 5.10. Two clusters dominate: the Highway 18 crags, which include Castle Rock and Fisherman's Buttress, and the Mill Creek Road and Skyline Drive area, home to Black Bluff, Arctic Temple and the Snow Summit Boulders. Some crags offer wide views of the lake and surrounding peaks, and winter brings snow to the higher ground.

ca_lee_vining_canyon_tioga_road.blurb: Climbing along about ten miles of the road running west from Lee Vining toward Tioga Pass, at the northern end of the Eastern Sierra. Trad leads, with sport close behind, plus bouldering, a winter ice and mixed scene, alpine routes and some scrambling. Rock grades center on 5.10 and 5.11, and the ice is mostly WI3 to WI5, often one or two pitches. The Tioga Cliff area is a southeast-facing wall near 9,200 feet, mostly bolted and fairly hard, in the sun until about 1:30 p.m. Lee Vining Bouldering, the ice venues and Transpire Wall add variety. Cliffs are best in warmer months and are often empty.
